card.questionRef: 2015 OL Q2(a) — filling the cavity with insulation
card.stem: The sketch shows a dwelling house which was built over 40 years ago. The external wall is a 300 mm concrete block wall with a 100 mm cavity. There is no insulation in the cavity. It is proposed to insulate the external wall by: filling the cavity with insulation and adding an external system of insulation to the wall.
card.questionText: It is proposed to insulate the external wall by: filling the cavity with insulation. Using notes and freehand sketches, show the steps to be followed in applying each system of insulation to the wall.

rows.verbatim: Filling the cavity with insulation – Notes
rows.contextNote: Three valid steps, 4 marks each. Typical procedure (carried out by specialist firms): 22 mm diameter holes are drilled through the external leaf, usually spaced about 800 mm horizontally and 1350 mm vertically; special care is taken at damp proof courses and at heads of windows and doors, with extra holes drilled around openings so the cavity fills properly; polystyrene beads are pumped into the cavity while a light coating of glue is applied, setting into a solid structure; when pumping is complete the holes are filled. Other valid steps are acceptable.

rows.verbatim: Filling the cavity with insulation – Sketches
rows.contextNote: Quality of sketches for the cavity-fill steps: excellent 8, good 6, fair 4. The scheme sketches show the drill entering the outer leaf and the hole spacing on the wall.

card.questionText: Explain, with the aid of notes and freehand sketches, any five of the following: box dovetail joint; triple glazing; solar panel; cordless drill; skirting board; compression fitting; natural seasoning; concrete lintel; radon barrier.

rows.contextNote: Explain any five of the nine terms. Each term is marked separately: primary communication of relevant information 6 and other communication 4, in notes or sketches (the scheme reserves no fixed split between them). Box dovetail joint: a joint for box shapes and a common joint in high-quality furniture, made by hand or with special jigs; the slope of the dovetails matters for strength, usually 1:6 in softwood and 1:8 in hardwood; it gives a decorative appearance, sometimes highlighted with contrasting woods. A sketch should show the interlocking tails and pins at the corner. Triple glazing: three panes of glass with a cavity between each; a better insulator and better acoustic performance than double glazing; low-e coatings reflect heat back into the house; cavities filled with argon or krypton reduce heat loss; an improved window U-value, a more comfortable indoor temperature and reduced condensation. A sketch should show the three panes, spacers and cavities. Solar panel: a solar collector absorbs solar radiation and converts it to heat, usually on a south-facing roof or secure ground-level fixing, working with other forms of heating and reducing CO2 emissions; types include flat-plate and evacuated-tube collectors, and tubes can be mounted to follow the sun. The scheme also lists photovoltaic panels: a coherent explanation of either is acceptable, but a photovoltaic panel produces electricity, not heat. Cordless drill: battery operated with rechargeable batteries, so not directly connected to AC mains power in use; features similar to a mains drill, including hammer action; used for driving screws, with a clutch to prevent damage to screw heads; right-angle versions for tight spaces; several power and speed settings, light low-voltage drills for DIY and heavier higher-voltage drills for robust work. A sketch should show the drill body, chuck and battery. Skirting board: a decorative board fitted at the junction of a wall and floor, giving a neat finish; hardwood, softwood or MDF in various lengths and profiles; typical sections from 100 mm × 15 mm to 200 mm × 20 mm; mitred at internal and external corners. A sketch should show the board fixed at the wall–floor junction. Compression fitting: a plumbing joint for copper or PVC pipes, made of brass or PVC in a range of sizes; the pipe ends are cut square, the nut and olive are fitted over the pipe, the pipe is pushed into the fitting and the nut is tightened to compress the olive into a watertight joint; PTFE tape may be used. A sketch should show the body, nut, olive and pipe. Natural seasoning: a traditional method of reducing the moisture content of timber; planks are stacked parallel with spaces between, separated by stickers (usually about 25 mm × 15 mm), in an open shed on a clean, dry, level base such as brick piers, and dried by the prevailing weather; plank ends are painted to prevent splitting; one species per stack; moisture content falls to about 18–22%, in equilibrium with the surrounding air; cheap because it uses no electrical energy, but slow and the rate cannot be controlled. A sketch should show the stacked planks, stickers and cover. Concrete lintel: a reinforced concrete beam spanning a door or window opening, carrying the blockwork or brickwork above and transferring the load to the wall at either side; cast in situ or, more commonly, pre-stressed; the length depends on the opening width and the imposed loads, and pre-stressed lintels come in a range of lengths and widths. A sketch should show the lintel bearing on the wall either side of the opening. Radon barrier: a flexible membrane placed under the floor and extended through the external walls to prevent radon gas entering the building; fitted over the whole floor area as one complete, unbroken layer with all joints taped and sealed, including around service pipes; usually laid over sand blinding (which protects it) and beneath the insulation; it replaces the damp proof membrane; installed with care by trained personnel so it is not damaged. Only a membrane rated and detailed as a radon barrier does this job.
